From debugging to testing
Regression tests help catch previously fixed bugs when they recur
Debugging
Diagnoses the cause of an observed failure.
Testing
Checks expected behavior, manually or with
automation.
The regression-test habit
•Write a reproducing test before the fix whenever feasible. Confirm it fails for the expected
reason.
•Fix the code, then run the regression test and the wider suite.
•Retain the test while its behavior remains part of the contract.
•If reproduction is unreliable, document the conditions and add the best repeatable check.
Unit testing basics: Arrange –Act –Assert
A C unit test checks one function behavior using controlled input
Arrange
Create a small input array. Replace hardware or file access with
a stub C function when needed.
Act
Call the C function once and store its return value.
Assert
Use assert(actual == expected) to check the result.
Use a descriptive C test name, such as test_sum_three_values. Keep tests fast and independent. Compile
assert-based tests without NDEBUG, otherwise their checks disappear. Test file and device access separately
with controlled dependencies.
Your first C unit test, line by line
Contract: n ≥ 0. For n > 0, provide n readable ints. Every intermediate sum must fit int.
C code in test_sum.c
What it does
Beginner trap to avoid
#include <assert.h>
int sum(int *, int);
Includes assert macro.
Declares sum().
Link sum_lib.c, without a main().
int main(void) {
int a[] = {10,20,30};
Arrange: three known input
values.
Keep the input deterministic.
int actual = sum(a, 3);
Act: call sum() once.
Pass the correct array length.
assert(actual == 60);
Assert: verify the expected sum.
Do not define NDEBUG for this test.
return 0; }
Exit 0 after a passing check.
Make the expected value wrong once.
Build: gcc test_sum.c sum_lib.c -o test_sum
Run: ./test_sum (sum_lib.c contains sum() only; see notes.)
Worked lab: a missed element in sum()
Illustrative defect: the loop skips the final value. Keep the expected result unchanged.
1 Reproduce the defect
int total = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
total += values[i];
}
return total;
2 Observe the failure
int a[] = {10, 20, 30};
int actual = sum(a, 3);
assert(actual == 60);
Actual: 30 Expected: 60
The assertion fails.
3 Fix the loop bound, then rerun the same test
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) Actual: 60. Test passes.
Run the full suite next.
Test case design: choosing the few tests that matter
Exhaustive testing is usually impractical for realistic input spaces
Technique
Idea
C example to exercise
Equivalence partitioning
Test representative input classes.
parse_int(): "42", "abc", "".
Boundary values
Test just below, at and above a limit.
For capacity 4: lengths 3, 4 and 5.
Decision table
Combine independent conditions.
enabled and valid: all 4 combinations.
State transition
Test allowed and rejected transitions.
enum state: CLOSED, OPEN; read while
CLOSED.
Negative testing
Use invalid inputs only if the API promises
safe rejection.
NULL buffer, negative length, bad file
path.
Coverage shows exercised code. Strong tests also need meaningful assertions and risk-based input choices.
Worked cases for the same sum() function
Use the contract to choose inputs and write the expected result before running the test.
Case
Input and expected result
Why this case matters
Zero elements
{7}, n = 0: expect 0
Checks the empty range.
Single element
{7}, n = 1: expect 7
Catches a skipped last element.
Mixed signs
{
-3,5,-2}, n = 3: expect 0
Checks addition with cancellation.
Normal case
{10,20,30}, n = 3: expect 60
Reproduces the worked defect.
All cases respect the contract. Invalid pointers and overflowing sums are outside this API’s promise.
The test pyramid: where your tests should live
Illustrative mix by test count: many unit tests and fewer broad tests. Adapt to risk.
End-to-end · ~10%
Run the complete C executable
through its command-line interface
with known input and output.
Integration · ~20%
Link parser.c with storage.c. Test file
formats, return codes and
ownership across both modules.
Unit · ~70%
Test sum() with a fixed array,
without files or devices. Run it on
every commit.
A suite dominated by broad tests can increase runtime, maintenance and flakiness.
Classify by scope and dependencies. Investigate slow tests separately.
Integration mindset for medium-scale projects
Modules that each work perfectly can still fail together
Contracts first
Define function prototypes in .h
files. Agree pointer ownership,
buffer sizes, units and error
returns before implementation.
Test the seams
Test C module boundaries:
struct fields, byte order, buffer
lengths and allocation/free
responsibilities.
Fake the neighbours
Use stubs to control
dependencies. They check a
simulated contract. Also test
with real dependencies.
Assume failure
Simulate fopen() returning NULL
or a driver reporting timeout.
Check cleanup and the returned
status.
Integrate continuously
Merge small changes often.
Frequent integration exposes
compatibility problems earlier.
Observability is part of done
Log function names, input sizes
and return codes. Capture a core
dump when an approved test
process crashes.
A C stub controls the input to sum()
Same project, new boundary: read three values, then sum them only when the read succeeds.
Production wrapper (excerpt)
int read_total(int (*read3)(int *),
int *out) {
int a[3];
int rc = read3(a);
if (rc != 0) return rc;
*out = sum(a, 3);
return 0;
}
Stub behavior and checks
ok: writes {10,20,30}, returns 0
timeout: writes nothing, returns -1
int out = 99;
assert(read_total(ok, &out) == 0);
assert(out == 60);
On timeout: expect status -1 and out unchanged at 99. No resource cleanup is needed here.
Full stubs and runnable tests are in the notes. Also test the real reader separately.
One command runs the suite locally and in CI
Illustrative GitHub Actions setup. Keep the C files and test.sh in the repository root.
.github/workflows/c-tests.yml
name: C tests
on: [push, pull_request]
permissions:
contents: read
jobs:
c-tests:
runs-on: ubuntu-latest
steps:
- uses: actions/checkout@v4
- run: bash test.sh
test.sh
set -eu
gcc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra \
-UNDEBUG test_sum.c \
sum_lib.c -o test_sum
./test_sum
test_sum.c runs four named cases.
RUN identifies each case.
PASS appears after its check.
Full runner code: speaker notes.
After the first run, make c-tests a required merge check in repository rules.
What this looks like on a real team
Your laptop is not the last place code is tested
•On each push, compile with warnings and run the
tests.
•Make the test job a required merge check.
Propagate every test failure to the job.
•Review buffer bounds, pointer ownership and error
returns.
•Investigate intermittent failures rather than
rerunning until green.
Lab completion checklist
•Show the failing reproducer, the fix and all four cases passing.
•Show that a failing required CI check blocks the merge. Restore the fix and rerun.

Unit testing
with GoogleTest
Basics and hands-on practice
C++ tests for the existing C implementation
Unit-testing basics with GoogleTest
Test one observable behavior with controlled inputs and an explicit expected result.
The test stays small
Arrange known input and dependencies.
Act on the function or component.
Check its result and relevant side effects.
Keep cases independent and repeatable.
GoogleTest supplies the runner
TEST groups named cases into suites.
EXPECT_* and ASSERT_* report failures.
Filters run one case or one suite.
Fixtures reuse setup without test-order
dependence.
A framework improves execution and diagnostics. You still choose the cases and expected behavior.
C code and C++ tests share a C-compatible header
Keep sum_lib.c compiled as C. Compile the GoogleTest source as C++.
sum.h
#ifndef SUM_H
#define SUM_H
#ifdef __cplusplus
extern "C" {
#endif
int sum(int *values, int n);
#ifdef __cplusplus
}
#endif
#endif
Project files
sum.h
Shared declaration with C linkage
sum_lib.c
Existing C implementation, no main()
test_sum_gtest.cpp
C++ tests, #include "sum.h"
Link both with GTest::gtest_main.
Do not link the old test_sum.c main().
The first GoogleTest cases for sum()
test_sum_gtest.cpp replaces the hand-written test runner, while the C function stays the same.
#include <gtest/gtest.h>
#include "sum.h"
TEST(Sum, AddsThreeValues) {
int a[] = {10, 20, 30};
int actual = sum(a, 3);
EXPECT_EQ(60, actual);
}
TEST(Sum, ZeroElements) {
int a[] = {7};
EXPECT_EQ(0, sum(a, 0));
}
Read the test name
Sum is the test suite.
AddsThreeValues is the case.
Use descriptive names that explain
the behavior.
Add SingleElement and MixedSigns
next.
All four cases are in the notes.
EXPECT and ASSERT control failure handling
Choose a fatal check when later statements cannot safely continue.
Check
What a failure does
Typical use
EXPECT_EQ(a, b)
Records failure; continues this function.
Independent value checks.
ASSERT_NE(p, nullptr)
Records failure; returns from this function.
Guard before dereferencing p.
EXPECT_STREQ(a, b)
Compares C
-string contents.
Use for text, not pointer equality.
EXPECT_NEAR(a, b, tol)
Checks absolute difference against tol.
Choose a justified numeric tolerance.
ASSERT_* stops the current function, not the whole suite. In a helper, it returns only from that helper.
CMake builds C code and C++ tests together
Host lab: C and C++17 toolchains, CMake 3.20+, a build tool, and access to the pinned dependency.
1 Configure the dependency
project(sum_tests LANGUAGES C CXX)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)
include(FetchContent)
# Declare pinned GoogleTest URL.
# Full declaration is in the notes.
FetchContent_MakeAvailable(googletest)
2 Register the test target
enable_testing()
add_library(sum_lib sum_lib.c)
add_executable(sum_tests
test_sum_gtest.cpp)
target_link_libraries(sum_tests
PRIVATE sum_lib GTest::gtest_main)
include(GoogleTest)
gtest_discover_tests(sum_tests)
Excerpts above. Complete CMakeLists.txt and the pinned dependency are in the speaker notes.
Fixtures reuse setup while keeping tests independent
Use TEST_F when several cases need the same setup. Simple cases can stay as TEST.
#include <gtest/gtest.h>
#include "sum.h"
class SumFixture : public ::testing::Test {
protected:
int a[3] = {10, 20, 30};
};
TEST_F(SumFixture, AddsInitialValues) {
EXPECT_EQ(60, sum(a, 3));
}
TEST_F(SumFixture, HandlesChangedInput) {
a[0] = -10;
EXPECT_EQ(40, sum(a, 3));
}
A fresh fixture per test
GoogleTest creates a new fixture
for each case.
Changing a in one test does not
alter the next fixture.
Use SetUp() and TearDown() for
shared setup and cleanup logic.
Run, diagnose and automate the GoogleTest suite
Use the same four cases and the same missed-last-element defect from the first module.
Build and run on a host
cmake -S . -B build
cmake --build build
ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure
# Run one case (Unix single-config build)
./build/sum_tests \
--gtest_filter=Sum.AddsThreeValues
Lab completion
1 Run all four cases.
2 Reintroduce i < n - 1.
3 Read the failing case and values.
4 Restore i < n and rerun.
CI: run configure, build and CTest as required checks.
Expected lab outcome: the defect fails three cases; the corrected function passes all four.
Complete example: the C implementation
Create one folder, sum_demo. Keep all four files from this example in that folder.
File 1: sum.h
#ifndef SUM_H
#define SUM_H
#ifdef __cplusplus
extern "C" {
#endif
int sum(int *values, int n);
#ifdef __cplusplus
}
#endif
#endif
File 2: sum_lib.c
#include "sum.h"
int sum(int *values, int n) {
int total = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
total += values[i];
}
return total;
}
Contract: n ≥ 0, with n readable ints when n > 0. Every intermediate sum must fit int.
The function does not validate input. The tests below stay within this contract.
Complete example: all four GoogleTest cases
File 3: test_sum_gtest.cpp. Copy the left column, then the right column into the same file.
Start of file
#include <gtest/gtest.h>
#include "sum.h"
TEST(Sum, AddsThreeValues) {
int a[] = {10, 20, 30};
EXPECT_EQ(60, sum(a, 3));
}
TEST(Sum, ZeroElements) {
int a[] = {7};
EXPECT_EQ(0, sum(a, 0));
}
Continuation
TEST(Sum, SingleElement) {
int a[] = {7};
EXPECT_EQ(7, sum(a, 1));
}
TEST(Sum, MixedSigns) {
int a[] = {-3, 5, -2};
EXPECT_EQ(0, sum(a, 3));
}
GTest::gtest_main supplies main().
Do not add the earlier test_sum.c.
No fixture is required for this example.
Complete example: the full CMake configuration
File 4: CMakeLists.txt. Read down the left column, then continue at the top right.
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(sum_demo LANGUAGES C CXX)
set(CMAKE_C_STANDARD 17)
set(CMAKE_C_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)
include(FetchContent)
set(GTEST_BASE
"https://github.com/google/googletest")
FetchContent_Declare(googletest
URL "${GTEST_BASE}/archive/refs/tags/v1.17.0.zip"
)
set(gtest_force_shared_crt ON
CACHE BOOL "" FORCE)
FetchContent_MakeAvailable(googletest)
enable_testing()
add_library(sum_lib sum_lib.c)
target_include_directories(sum_lib
PUBLIC ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR})
add_executable(sum_tests test_sum_gtest.cpp)
target_link_libraries(sum_tests
PRIVATE sum_lib GTest::gtest_main)
include(GoogleTest)
gtest_discover_tests(sum_tests)
Prerequisites: compatible C/C++17 compilers, CMake 3.20+, a build tool and dependency access.
GoogleTest v1.17.0 is pinned for this lab. Use an approved mirror if network access is restricted.
Complete example: build, fail and fix
Run these commands from sum_demo. Expected results below are illustrative, not captured logs.
Configure, build and run
cmake -S . -B build
cmake --build build
ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure
Make one deliberate change
In sum_lib.c, replace i < n with i < n - 1.
Rebuild, then rerun CTest.
Restore i < n, rebuild and run again.
Expected result
Correct code
4 passed, 0 failed
Skipped final element
1 passed, 3 failed
Restored code
4 passed, 0 failed
